title: What Is Arthritis? Symptoms, Types and Next Steps

direct_answer: Arthritis causes joint pain, swelling or stiffness, but it is not one diagnosis. Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis and gout differ in cause and treatment. See a GP for unexplained symptoms lasting more than a few days. A suddenly very painful, hot or swollen joint needs urgent GP or NHS 111 advice.
author: Louis Maxwell
keywords: what is arthritis, arthritis symptoms, types of arthritis
content:
Arthritis means a condition affecting one or more joints, usually causing pain, swelling or stiffness and making movement harder. It is a broad label, not one diagnosis. Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis and gout have different causes and may need quite different treatment.

If someone has told you that you have arthritis, the most useful next question is: which type? If you have not been assessed, do not assume that a sore or swollen joint is simply arthritis or a normal part of getting older. This guide explains what the word means, what to tell your GP and which symptoms need urgent help.

What happens in a joint with arthritis?

A joint is where bones meet. Cartilage helps the ends of the bones move smoothly, while the joint lining and surrounding tissues support movement. Different types of arthritis affect these structures in different ways. Pain alone does not show which structure is involved or identify the cause.

Arthritis can affect hands, feet, knees, hips or the spine, among other joints. Symptoms may vary from day to day. A flare means symptoms have become worse, but a new hot or very painful joint should not automatically be treated as your usual flare.

How do the main types differ?

  • Osteoarthritis: the most common type in the UK. Changes in the cartilage and other joint tissues can cause pain, stiffness and difficulty moving. Knees, hips and small hand joints are often affected. It is not inevitable that symptoms will keep getting worse.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis: an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks the joint lining. It often affects the hands, feet and wrists and can also cause fatigue or problems elsewhere in the body. Early treatment can reduce the risk of joint damage.
  • Gout: a type of arthritis linked to uric acid crystals around a joint. It often causes sudden severe pain, heat and swelling, commonly in the big toe but sometimes elsewhere. A first attack needs assessment because infection can cause similar symptoms.
  • Other types: psoriatic arthritis may occur with psoriasis; ankylosing spondylitis often affects the back; juvenile idiopathic arthritis affects children. The NHS arthritis overview describes these types.

These are explanations, not a way to diagnose yourself from the location of pain. More than one problem can affect the same person, and symptoms can overlap.

Which symptoms should you mention?

Tell the GP about pain, visible swelling, warmth, stiffness and changes in movement. Explain what you can no longer do comfortably, such as opening a jar, walking to the shop or getting dressed. Fatigue, a rash, eye symptoms or feeling generally unwell can also matter.

Osteoarthritis often causes symptoms around activity. Rheumatoid arthritis can cause prolonged stiffness after waking or resting and often affects several small joints. Neither pattern proves a diagnosis. The NHS rheumatoid arthritis symptoms guide also notes that symptoms do not always affect both sides equally.

When does joint pain need urgent help?

Ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 if you have sudden severe pain and swelling in one joint, a hot or red joint, or sore joints with a high or low temperature or feeling hot, cold or shivery. Redness can be harder to see on brown or black skin. Joint pain with sore eyes or changes in vision also needs urgent assessment.

Septic arthritis is a serious joint infection that needs treatment quickly. Not everyone has a fever. Do not wait for a routine appointment, try an exercise programme or assume a new hot swollen joint is gout without getting advice.

The NHS also advises urgent help if joint pain is not relieved by painkillers, or if sore joints occur with pain when passing urine, genital discharge, or genital sores or a rash. The NHS arthritis page gives the full urgent-help list.

Call 111 in England, Scotland or Wales when appropriate. In Northern Ireland, contact your GP or GP out-of-hours service. For a life-threatening emergency, call 999.

When should you book a routine GP appointment?

Book a GP appointment for unexplained joint pain, swelling or stiffness that does not go away in a few days. Do not wait until pain is severe or until you cannot work. Seek assessment sooner if the urgent signs above occur.

Persistent swelling of small hand or foot joints, or several joints, is especially important to mention. NICE recommends specialist assessment for suspected persistent joint-lining inflammation, with urgent referral in specified circumstances. Normal blood tests do not remove the need for referral when the clinician suspects this. You do not need to decide which blood test to request before asking for help.

How is the type of arthritis diagnosed?

A clinician will ask about your symptoms and medical history and examine the joints. Depending on the suspected cause, tests may include blood tests, an X-ray or ultrasound, or a sample of joint fluid. Not everyone needs all of these tests.

Osteoarthritis is often diagnosed from the history and examination without an X-ray or blood test. Rheumatoid arthritis assessment may involve blood tests and a rheumatology referral. Gout sometimes needs a joint-fluid sample or further tests when the diagnosis is unclear. A scan result or a single blood result is not a complete explanation on its own.

What treatment and support can help?

Treatment depends on the type of arthritis and how it affects you. It may include exercise or physiotherapy, occupational therapy for everyday tasks, medicines, suitable aids and, in some cases, surgery. Rheumatoid arthritis medicines may also aim to slow the disease and reduce joint damage, rather than only relieving pain.

Exercise is an important part of osteoarthritis care, including strengthening and general fitness. Build up gradually and follow an individual plan if you have one. New severe pain, heat or swelling needs assessment rather than pushing through it. Ask a pharmacist or clinician before choosing pain medicines, especially if you take other medicines or have other health conditions.

There is no single diet, supplement or exercise that treats every type of arthritis. Do not stop prescribed treatment because a different approach sounds promising. Ask what the treatment is intended to do, when it will be reviewed and whom to contact if symptoms change.

What should you take to an appointment?

  • Which joints are affected and when the symptoms started.
  • Whether swelling, warmth or stiffness comes and goes, and roughly how long morning stiffness lasts.
  • Tasks, work, sleep or walking that have become difficult.
  • Other symptoms, including fatigue, psoriasis, eye symptoms or feeling unwell.
  • A list of medicines and supplements and what you have already tried.

A short note or photograph of swelling that comes and goes may help explain the problem. It cannot rule out infection and should never delay urgent assessment.

Key takeaways

  • Arthritis is a broad term. The type matters because causes and treatment differ.
  • Unexplained joint symptoms lasting more than a few days deserve a GP assessment.
  • A suddenly very painful, hot or swollen joint needs urgent advice, even without a fever.
  • Ask for a clear diagnosis, a workable treatment plan and instructions for changing symptoms.

Frequently asked questions

Is arthritis just getting older?

No. Risk varies by type, and arthritis can affect younger adults and children. New symptoms should not be dismissed because of your age.

Can you tell the type from a painful joint?

No. Location and symptom pattern help a clinician decide what to check, but they do not confirm a diagnosis by themselves.

Does everyone need an X-ray?

No. Osteoarthritis can often be diagnosed without imaging. Tests depend on the suspected cause and the findings at examination.

Can normal blood tests rule out rheumatoid arthritis?

No. NICE says suspected persistent joint-lining inflammation may still need specialist referral despite normal or negative blood tests.

Can exercise replace arthritis medicines?

No. Movement can support symptoms and function, but it does not replace disease-controlling treatment when that is needed. Discuss treatment changes with your clinical team.

Your next step

If symptoms are new, use the urgent signs above to decide whether to seek help now or book a GP appointment. If arthritis is already diagnosed, check that you know the type, what each treatment is for and what to do during a change in symptoms.
